title: Short analysis essays
specPoints: Component 3 Section B: extended response comparison

tips.title: Both pieces, or half the marks are gone
tips.body: The mark scheme says in plain words that a mark **cannot go above the top of level 2** if only one piece has been considered. The top of level 2 is **6**. So an answer that covers one extract brilliantly and forgets the other scores at most half of 12, however good it is.

tips.title: A judgement needs a feature attached to it
tips.body: The mark scheme states that an AO4 point is credited only where there is a corresponding AO3 observation. "It sounds exciting" earns nothing on its own. "The syncopated bass line makes it sound restless" earns on both halves, because the feature is named and then judged.

tips.title: Plan by element, never by piece
tips.body: Two paragraphs, one per piece, produce two descriptions and no comparison, and comparison is where AO4 lives. Take one element at a time — texture, then melody, then harmony — and say what each piece does with it in the same breath. The comparison then writes itself.

tips.title: Other music you know earns credit here
tips.body: The specification says credit is given where students refer to other music, from the suggested wider listening or anything else relevant they have studied. One accurate sentence placing your set work beside another piece of its period is worth having ready for every area of study.

why.matters: Section B is one question, twelve marks, fifteen per cent of the paper and six per cent of the whole GCSE, on one page of writing about two pieces: a set work and an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study, played alternately. The marks come in four levels, and the wall most answers hit is between level 2 and level 3, where three things change at once: both pieces rather than one, evidence rather than assertion, and analysis rather than description. Plan by element, not by piece, and the comparison writes itself.

examples.title: Six per cent of the grade on one page
examples.body: Section A is 68 marks and Section B is 12. Twelve of eighty is fifteen per cent of the paper, and since the paper is forty per cent of the qualification, that one answer is six per cent of the whole GCSE. It is worth planning for exactly the time it earns: three or four paragraphs, one per element, each naming both pieces, and a conclusion.

examples.title: Purcell against a jazz standard
examples.body: A real paper set *Music for a While*, from the 1690s, against a jazz standard recorded in the 1930s. What they share is the area of study, vocal music, not the century, and the comparison works because it is done element by element: in texture, one voice over a continuo against layered vocal parts; in word setting, syllabic lines with a painted word against whatever the standard does with its words. The differences are the argument. The essay is not two descriptions; it is one judgement made three or four times.

steps.title: One question, twelve marks, two pieces
steps.body:
Section B is a single question. It is worth **12 marks**, which is **15%** of the paper and, since Component 3 is 40% of the qualification, **6%** of the whole GCSE. One question, one page of writing, six per cent of your grade.

Here is exactly what happens.

- You are given **one set work** extract and **one unfamiliar** extract. The unfamiliar piece relates to one of the set works.
- **Scores for both** are printed in a separate **source booklet**.
- They are played **alternately**: familiar, unfamiliar, familiar, unfamiliar, familiar, unfamiliar. Three hearings of each.
- The question names what to compare — melody and texture, say — and uses a command word such as *evaluate* or *compare*.

The two pieces will not always be from the same period. A real paper set Purcell's *Music for a While*, from the 1690s, against a jazz standard recorded in the 1930s. What they share is the area of study, not the century.

> The specification also promises credit for referring to **other music you have studied** — the suggested wider listening, or anything else relevant.

steps.title: Two halves: knowing, and judging
steps.body:
The 12 marks are split down the middle.

- **AO3, 6 marks** — demonstrating and applying musical knowledge. Naming features, using the right vocabulary, supporting points with evidence from the score.
- **AO4, 6 marks** — using appraising skills to make evaluative and critical judgements. Saying what the feature *does*, comparing, concluding.

And then the rule that decides most answers:

> The mark scheme states that **AO4 can only be credited if there is a corresponding AO3 observation**.

Read that as a sentence pattern. Every point you make has two halves, and the first one has to come first.

**Feature → effect.**

| Earns nothing | Earns on both halves |
| --- | --- |
| It sounds exciting | The syncopated bass makes it sound restless |
| It is a sad piece | The minor tonality gives it a lamenting quality |
| I preferred the second extract | The second extract's wider range lets the singer sound more desperate |
| There is a lot going on | The three independent lines make the texture feel crowded |

The left column is pure AO4 with nothing underneath it, and it is credited at nothing. The right column is the same judgement with a feature attached, and it earns in both columns of the mark scheme.

The reverse mistake is quieter and just as expensive. A page of accurate observations with no judgements anywhere gives away all 6 AO4 marks and cannot get past level 2, because the level descriptors are written in terms of appraisal as well as knowledge.

steps.title: The four levels, and the trap in level 2
steps.body:
The twelve marks are awarded in **four levels of three marks each**.

- **Level 1, 1 to 3.** A few isolated points about one or both extracts. Little or no musical vocabulary. Appraisal basic and undeveloped.
- **Level 2, 4 to 6.** Points about one or both extracts, with little supporting evidence. Some basic vocabulary. Similarities and differences covered, but mainly by describing them.
- **Level 3, 7 to 9.** Points about **both** extracts, with evidence, and some awareness of style. A good range of vocabulary. Straightforward analysis of similarities and differences, and some attempt at conclusions.
- **Level 4, 10 to 12.** Points about **both** extracts, fully supported by evidence, with stylistic awareness of both. Extensive and sophisticated vocabulary. A cohesive critical argument, comparing, contrasting and drawing conclusions.

Now look at what changes between level 2 and level 3. Three things, all at once: **both** pieces rather than either, **evidence** rather than assertion, and **analysis** rather than description. That is the wall, and it is where most answers stop.

And printed against level 2 in the mark scheme is this:

> "The mark awarded cannot progress beyond the top of this band if only ONE piece has been considered."

The top of level 2 is **6**. So an answer about one piece is capped at 6 out of 12 — **exactly half** — no matter how good it is. A brilliant page on the set work with two lines tacked on about the unfamiliar piece is not a level 4 answer with a small omission. It is a level 2 answer.

steps.title: Plan by element, not by piece
steps.body:
There are two ways to organise a comparison, and only one of them works.

**The way that fails.** A paragraph on the set work, then a paragraph on the unfamiliar piece. It feels organised. It produces two descriptions and no comparison, so the AO4 marks for comparing, contrasting and drawing conclusions have nowhere to land. It also makes it very easy to run out of time and leave the second piece with three lines — which caps the whole answer at 6.

**The way that works.** One paragraph per **musical element**, each one carrying both pieces.

> In **texture**, Purcell writes for a single voice over a continuo, so one line is always in charge; the second extract layers three vocal parts in harmony from its second repetition, so the ear has no single line to follow. Both thicken towards the end, but Purcell does it by decorating one line and the song does it by adding parts.

That is one paragraph. It names both pieces, it compares rather than describes, and it ends on a judgement about how they differ. Three or four of those, and a conclusion, is a full answer.

**Choosing the elements.** The question names its focus — *melody and texture*, say. Take those first. If the question is more open, pick three or four from this list and leave the rest alone.

- Sonority
- Texture
- Melody
- Tonality and harmony
- Rhythm and metre
- Structure
- Dynamics
- Context

Three elements done properly beats eight done in a line each. The level 4 descriptor asks for a **cohesive critical argument**, and an argument needs room.

steps.title: Evidence is what the scores are for
steps.body:
Both score extracts are printed in the source booklet. The level descriptors mention evidence three times, and at level 4 points must be **fully supported by** it. So what counts?

- **A bar number.** "The bass falls chromatically in bars 1 to 3" is evidence. "The bass falls" is not.
- **A named pitch or chord.** "The E7 at the end of each pattern" is evidence. "The last chord" is weaker.
- **A count.** "Repeated seven times", "three vocal parts", "an eleven-note melisma". Numbers are cheap to write and hard to argue with.
- **A named instrument or voice.** "Fretless bass", "solo oboe", "harpsichord and bass viol".
- **A quoted word of text**, in vocal music. Word-painting cannot be discussed without it.

Put the four parts of a point in this order and they almost always work:

> **Name it. Locate it. Say what it does. Then say how the other piece differs.**

> *Purcell's ground bass is **3 bars** long and entirely in quavers **(name it)**, repeating from bar 1 and breaking off only at **bar 14** **(locate it)**. Because it ends on **chord V**, each repetition resolves only when the next one starts, so the music never comes to rest **(what it does)**. The song's four-bar pattern works in exactly the same way — it ends on E7 and falls to A minor at the start of the next repetition — but it is diatonic rather than chromatic, so it circles comfortably where Purcell's ground keeps straining **(how the other differs)**.*

That is one point, four sentences, and it earns under both assessment objectives.

steps.title: A twelve-mark answer, worked
steps.body:
**The question.** The familiar extract is Purcell's *Music for a While*, from the Vocal Music area of study. **Extract B, unfamiliar.** A song for solo voice, electric piano, fretless bass and drum kit played with brushes.

**On the page:** no sharps or flats; four crotchets in a bar; a slow tempo. The chord symbols printed above the vocal line are Am | G | F | E7, and they repeat unchanged for the whole extract.

**What you hear:**

- The bass plays the same four-bar descending pattern — A, G, F, E — seven times over, with no break between repetitions.
- Each repetition ends on E7 and falls back to A minor at the start of the next.
- The first two repetitions are syllabic and stay within a sixth. From the third the voice becomes increasingly melismatic and adds flattened thirds and sevenths.
- The vocal line is different every time round; no repetition is sung the same way twice.
- The drums and electric piano drop out for the last repetition, leaving voice and bass alone.

**Evaluate how effectively each piece uses a repeating bass to sustain interest across the extract.**

Before writing, three decisions.

1. **Which elements?** The question names the repeating bass, so **structure** and **harmony** lead. **Melody** follows, because what happens above the bass is how each piece avoids monotony. That is enough.
2. **What is the comparison actually about?** Both pieces do the same structural thing four centuries apart. The interesting question is not *whether* they are similar but *how each one keeps it interesting*.
3. **What is the conclusion?** Decide it now. Here: both succeed, but by opposite means — Purcell varies what sits above a fixed bass, while the song varies the voice itself against a bass that has stopped asking for attention.

The answer below is organised by element and carries both pieces through each one.

visuals.problem: The finished answer, paragraph by paragraph.

steps.text: Structure. Both pieces are built on a repeating bass. Purcell uses a ground bass of three bars, entirely in quavers and arpeggio based, and Baroque composers used it exactly as the song uses its four-bar pattern of A, G, F and E: as the fixed frame for everything else.
steps.note: Both pieces named in the first sentence, with the AO3 observation stated for each. The one-piece cap is now out of reach.

steps.text: The crucial detail is where each pattern ends. Purcell’s ground closes on chord V, so it is unresolved until the next repetition begins; the song’s pattern closes on E7 and falls to A minor as the next one starts. In both, the join is the point of arrival, so the music cannot come to rest until the piece stops.
steps.note: One observation for each piece, then a judgement that applies to both. This is the comparison the question is really about.

steps.text: They differ in how strictly the frame holds. The song repeats its pattern seven times without a break. Purcell breaks his ground off at bar 14 to modulate, brings it back at bar 23 and reprises the opening at bar 29, so his structure has an arch that the song’s does not.
steps.note: A difference, evidenced with bar numbers, and named as a structural consequence rather than just a fact.

steps.text: Harmony. Purcell’s ground is chromatic and rises by semitones, so the tonality is often ambiguous and dissonances such as the false relation in bar 1 arise from the bass itself. The song’s Am, G, F, E7 is entirely diatonic and never varies, so its harmony asks for no attention at all.
steps.note: Named features on both sides; the vocabulary is specific — chromatic, false relation, diatonic.

steps.text: That difference decides where the interest has to come from. Purcell can let the bass generate tension; the song cannot, and so has to generate all of it in the voice.
steps.note: A judgement drawn from the observations, not asserted independently of them. This is the kind of sentence the level 4 descriptor calls a critical argument.

steps.text: Melody. Purcell varies the vocal line over the fixed ground, with word-painting on drop — nine descending notes on weak off-beats in bars 23 to 25 — and melismatic writing against syllabic elsewhere. The song’s singer never repeats a line the same way, moving from syllabic and within a sixth to increasingly melismatic with flattened thirds and sevenths.
steps.note: The same element in both, evidenced, with the vocabulary each tradition uses: word-painting for Purcell, blue notes for the song.

steps.text: Both, in other words, place the variety in the voice. Purcell also varies the continuo realisation beneath it, so he has two changing layers over one fixed one; the song has only one.
steps.note: A similarity, then a difference inside it. Comparisons that find a difference inside a similarity read as analysis rather than description.

steps.text: Context. The ground bass was a Baroque commonplace and Purcell was regarded as a master of it; a repeating chord loop is equally standard in modern popular song. Handel’s and Pachelbel’s grounds do what Purcell’s does, and countless songs do what this one does.
steps.note: Stylistic awareness of both pieces, which the level 3 and 4 descriptors both require, plus the wider-listening reference the specification credits.

steps.text: Conclusion. Both sustain interest effectively, but by opposite routes. Purcell’s chromatic ground keeps the harmony unsettled and the interest is shared between voice and continuo; the song’s diatonic loop is deliberately unremarkable, so that everything the listener attends to is in the singing. The song is the more effective of the two at directing attention, and Purcell the more effective at sustaining tension.
steps.note: A conclusion that answers the question asked — how effectively — and makes a judgement about each piece rather than summarising.

It shows the answer will be long enough for twelve marks
It repeats the wording of the question back to the examiner
check.solution: An answer that considers only one piece is capped at **6 out of 12**. Writing about both from the very first paragraph removes that risk before time pressure can create it, which is the whole reason for organising by element rather than by piece.

steps.title: Context, wider listening and the command word
steps.body:
Three things sit outside the musical elements and are worth marks anyway.

**Context.** Both the level 3 and level 4 descriptors ask for **stylistic awareness**. That means placing the music: period, style, purpose, audience, the circumstances it was written for. But context earns only when it explains something audible.

> *Written in 1692* earns little. *Written in 1692, as incidental music for a play, which is why the aria is short and self-contained and works over a single repeating bass* earns, because the date is doing work.

**Wider listening.** The specification says credit is given where students refer to other music, "from the suggested wider listening pieces or any other relevant works". One sentence is enough. Have one ready for each area of study, and make it a real comparison rather than a name drop.

**The command word.** Appendix 5 defines them, and Section B uses the top three.

| Command word | What it wants |
| --- | --- |
| Compare | similarities and differences, with relative judgements |
| Analyse | examine and dissect musical elements in detail, and how they combine to create an effect |
| Evaluate | judgements made against parameters, and conclusions drawn |

*Evaluate* is the strongest of the three and the commonest in Section B. It asks how **well** something is done, which means your answer has to take a position. "How effectively do these composers exploit melody and texture" is not answered by listing what they do with melody and texture. It is answered by saying which does it better, and why.

props.centre: One wider-listening sentence per area of study

boxes.title: Instrumental music
boxes.body: Vivaldi and Handel wrote concertos on the same ritornello principle; a Haydn or Mozart sonata shows the Classical style the Baroque gave way to.

boxes.title: Vocal music
boxes.body: Handel’s Messiah arias show the same Baroque word setting; a Beach Boys or Alicia Keys track shows what studio production added.

boxes.title: Stage and screen
boxes.body: Howard Shore’s Lord of the Rings cues use leitmotif as Williams does; Hairspray and Matilda show the musical theatre idiom.

boxes.title: Fusions
boxes.body: Buena Vista Social Club and Afro-Cuban jazz show two traditions meeting, as Capercaillie does with Celtic music and dance beats.

check.solution: Appendix 5 defines *evaluate* as making judgements against parameters and drawing conclusions. *Describe* asks only for points. So an *evaluate* question is not answered by listing what each composer does — it is answered by taking a position on how well they do it, and saying why.

markScheme.description: make judgements and draw conclusions

steps.title: What separates level 3 from level 4
steps.body:
Level 3 and level 4 read similarly. The differences are precise, and there are four of them.

**"Some evidence" becomes "fully supported by evidence."** At level 3 the good points are evidenced. At level 4 they all are. In practice that means no sentence in the answer asserts a musical fact without locating it.

**"Some stylistic awareness" becomes "stylistic awareness of both pieces."** Knowing your set work's period is level 3. Placing the unfamiliar piece in a tradition too — recognising a jazz walking bass, a modern chord loop, a Classical periodic phrase — is level 4.

**"A good range of musical vocabulary" becomes "extensive and sophisticated."** Sophisticated does not mean obscure. It means the exact word rather than the approximate one: *heterophony* rather than "they play it slightly differently"; *Tierce de Picardie* rather than "it ends on a major chord"; *melisma* rather than "a long note on one syllable".

**"Some attempt at comparing and drawing conclusions" becomes "a cohesive critical argument."** This is the real gap. A level 3 answer compares point by point and then stops. A level 4 answer has a position and the comparisons serve it.

The practical version of that last one: **decide your conclusion before you start writing**, then choose the comparisons that build towards it. An answer that discovers its own opinion in the last two lines reads as a list with a summary attached. An answer that knows where it is going reads as an argument.

One more thing separates the best answers. They **find a difference inside a similarity**. "Both use a repeating bass" is an observation anyone makes. "Both use a repeating bass, but Purcell's is chromatic and generates the tension itself, while the song's is deliberately plain so that all the interest can sit in the voice" is the same observation turned into an argument.

steps.title: What to carry into the exam
steps.body:
- Section B is **one question, 12 marks**: one **set work** against one **unfamiliar piece**, with **scores for both**, played **three times each, alternating**.
- **6 marks AO3** for knowledge, vocabulary and evidence; **6 marks AO4** for evaluation, comparison and conclusions.
- An AO4 point is credited **only where an AO3 observation supports it**. Name the feature, then judge it.
- Four levels, three marks each: L1 1–3, L2 4–6, L3 7–9, L4 10–12.
- **A one-piece answer is capped at 6 of 12** — exactly half. Write about both from the first paragraph.
- **Plan by element, not by piece.** Three or four elements, both pieces in each.
- **Evidence** means a bar number, a count, a named chord, pitch, instrument or word.
- **Context earns** when it explains something audible, and **wider listening earns** in one accurate sentence.
- **Decide the conclusion before writing**, and choose comparisons that build towards it.
- Look for a **difference inside a similarity**. That is what an argument sounds like.

boxes.title: Name it
boxes.body: The musical feature, in the right word. Ground bass, melisma, heterophony, Tierce de Picardie.

boxes.title: Locate it
boxes.body: A bar number, a count, a chord symbol, a word of text. This is the evidence the levels ask for.

boxes.title: Say what it does
boxes.body: The effect on the listener or on the music. This is the AO4 half, and it is now credited.

boxes.title: Say how the other differs
boxes.body: The comparison. Without it you have two descriptions, and the answer stalls at level 2.

Four for musical knowledge, eight for appraisal

Everything about the set work, then a brief comparison

Level 3
Level 4
Level 1
questions.solution: The four levels are level 1 at 1 to 3, level 2 at 4 to 6, level 3 at 7 to 9, level 4 at 10 to 12. Eight marks sits inside level 3, which requires points about **both** extracts, supported by evidence, with some stylistic awareness and some attempt at drawing conclusions.

questions.prompt: A short bass pattern repeats throughout a Baroque aria while the parts above it change, and it ends on chord V so that it resolves only when the next repetition begins. Give the two-word term for this device.

questions.prompt: Put these in the order they should appear when you make a single point in a Section B answer.
items: Name the musical feature, using the correct term
Locate it: a bar number, a count, a chord or a word of text
Say what the feature does to the music or the listener
Say how the other extract handles the same thing differently
Draw the judgement that follows for both pieces
questions.solution: The feature comes first because the mark scheme credits an appraising point only where a musical observation supports it — a judgement written before its evidence has nothing underneath it. Locating the feature is what turns an assertion into the evidence the levels require. The effect is the AO4 half of the point. The comparison and the judgement come last, because they need both pieces on the table first.

evidence before effect
comparison and judgement last

questions.prompt: The question is "Evaluate how effectively each composer uses texture." Which is the strongest final paragraph?
options: Purcell’s single line keeps every ornament audible, while the song’s layered harmony instead serves its hook
In conclusion, both extracts use texture in many different and interesting ways across the whole passage
To summarise, Purcell writes a continuo texture and the second extract adds three vocal parts in harmony
Overall I enjoyed the textures of the second extract more, because they sounded much fuller and richer
questions.solution: *Evaluate* asks for judgements made against parameters and conclusions drawn. The answer about *Purcell’s single line* judges each piece against a stated parameter — what the texture is for — and reaches a different verdict for each. The second says nothing; the third restates observations already made; the fourth is a preference, which is not a judgement against a parameter.

markScheme.description: the option judging each piece against a stated parameter

questions.prompt: Which of these is an AO3 observation rather than an AO4 judgement?
options: The ending sounds hopeful rather than resigned
The second extract is the more successful of the two
The voice sings eleven notes on a single syllable
The texture makes the chorus feel like an arrival
questions.solution: AO3 is demonstrating and applying musical knowledge: a fact about the music, in the right vocabulary, that can be checked against the score. Eleven notes on one syllable is a melisma, counted. The other three are all judgements — each would be credited under AO4, but only if an observation like the first one were placed beside it.

markScheme.description: the option stating a checkable musical fact

questions.prompt: Component 3 is worth 40% of the GCSE, and Section B is 12 of the 80 marks on that paper. What percentage of the whole GCSE does Section B carry? Give your answer as a whole number.
questions.solution: 12 out of 80 is 15% of the paper. The paper is 40% of the qualification, so Section B carries 15% of 40%, which is **6%** of the whole GCSE. One question, one page, six per cent of the grade.

markScheme.description: 12 of 80 is 15%, and 15% of 40% is 6%

questions.prompt:
A student writes this as their whole answer.

> "Purcell's piece is very sad and slow. It is Baroque music from a long time ago and it has a harpsichord. The other piece is more modern and has drums in it. I liked the second one better because it is easier to listen to. They are both in a minor key which makes them sad. Purcell's one has a bass that keeps going round and round."

The question was: "Evaluate how effectively each piece uses a repeating bass to sustain interest."

Identify the level this answer would reach and justify it, then rewrite two of its points so that they would be credited at level 4.
questions.solution:
**The level.** This answer sits at **level 1**, so 1 to 3 marks. Both extracts are mentioned, so the one-piece cap is not the problem; the problem is everything the level 1 descriptor lists. The points are isolated — sad, slow, has a harpsichord, has drums — and none is developed. There is almost no musical vocabulary: "a bass that keeps going round and round" is a description of a **ground bass** by someone who does not have the term. The appraisal is basic and undeveloped, and one of the two judgements offered is a preference rather than a judgement at all.

**What is specifically wrong.**

- **No evidence anywhere.** Not one bar number, count, chord or pitch, although both scores are printed in the source booklet. The level 3 descriptor requires evidence supporting the points and level 4 requires them all to be supported.
- **A preference in place of a judgement.** "I liked the second one better because it is easier to listen to" is not an evaluation. *Evaluate* asks for judgements made against parameters; ease of listening is not a musical parameter, and nothing in the music is offered as a reason.
- **Judgements with no feature attached.** "They are both in a minor key which makes them sad" is closer — a feature is named — but the effect is asserted, not explained, and the same minor key does two quite different things in these two pieces.
- **Context that does no work.** "Baroque music from a long time ago" earns almost nothing. The date matters only when it explains something audible.
- **No comparison.** Each piece is described separately. Nothing is set against anything.

**Two points rewritten.**

*Instead of "Purcell's one has a bass that keeps going round and round":*

> Purcell builds the aria on a **ground bass**: a three-bar pattern, entirely in quavers and arpeggio based, repeating from bar 1 and breaking off only at bar 14 to modulate. Because it ends on chord V, each repetition is unresolved until the next one begins, so the music is never allowed to settle. The song's four-bar pattern of A, G, F and E works the same way — its E7 falls to A minor as the next repetition starts — but it is diatonic where Purcell's is chromatic, so it circles comfortably while his keeps straining.

*Instead of "They are both in a minor key which makes them sad":*

> Both extracts are in **A minor**, but the minor mode is doing different work in each. Purcell's ground is chromatic and rises by semitones, so the tonality is often ambiguous and dissonances such as the false relation in bar 1 arise from the bass itself; the sorrow is built into the harmony. The song's harmony never varies from Am, G, F, E7, so the minor key is simply the frame, and all the expression is carried by the voice, which moves from syllabic within a sixth to increasingly melismatic with flattened thirds and sevenths.

**Why those versions reach level 4.** Each names the feature in the correct term, locates it in the score, says what it does, and then compares the two pieces on the same point — and the comparison finds a difference inside the similarity rather than stopping at "both use a repeating bass".

questions.prompt:
**Extract A, familiar.** Purcell: *Music for a While*, from the Vocal Music area of study.

**Extract B, unfamiliar.** A song for solo voice, electric piano, fretless bass and drum kit played with brushes.

**On the page:** no sharps or flats; four crotchets in a bar; a slow tempo. The chord symbols printed above the vocal line are Am | G | F | E7, and they repeat unchanged for the whole extract.

**What you hear:**

- The bass plays the same four-bar descending pattern — A, G, F, E — seven times over, with no break between repetitions.
- Each repetition ends on E7 and falls back to A minor at the start of the next.
- The first two repetitions are syllabic and stay within a sixth. From the third the voice becomes increasingly melismatic and adds flattened thirds and sevenths.
- The vocal line is different every time round; no repetition is sung the same way twice.
- The drums and electric piano drop out for the last repetition, leaving voice and bass alone.

Evaluate how effectively each piece uses a repeating bass to sustain interest across the extract.
questions.solution:
**Structure.** Both extracts are built on a repeating bass, and both use it as the fixed frame for everything above. Purcell's is a **ground bass**: three bars, entirely in quavers, arpeggio based, played by the harpsichord left hand and doubled by the bass viol. The song's is a four-bar pattern descending A, G, F, E in the fretless bass, repeated seven times without a break.

The decisive detail is where each pattern ends. Purcell's ground closes on **chord V**, so it is unresolved until the next repetition begins. The song's closes on **E7**, which falls to A minor as the next repetition starts. In both, the moment of arrival is the join, which means neither piece can come to rest until it stops altogether — the same device, four centuries apart, doing exactly the same job.

They differ in how strictly the frame holds. The song repeats its pattern seven times unbroken. Purcell breaks the ground off at **bar 14** to modulate, brings it back at **bar 23**, and reprises the opening material at **bar 29**, which anticipates the ternary *da capo* aria of later Baroque opera. So Purcell's structure has an arch, and the song's is a loop.

**Harmony.** Purcell's ground is **chromatic**, rising by semitones, and the tonality it produces is often ambiguous: the F sharp in the bass against the F natural in the harpsichord at bar 1 is a **false relation**, a dissonance generated by the bass itself. The song's Am, G, F, E7 is entirely **diatonic** and never varies at all.

That difference decides where each piece has to find its interest. Purcell's bass can generate tension on its own, so the voice above it has help. The song's bass, by design, asks for no attention whatsoever, which means every ounce of the expression has to come from the singing. The judgement is not that one harmony is better but that each has been chosen for what it makes possible.

**Melody.** Both put the variety in the voice. Purcell varies the vocal line continuously over the fixed ground and uses **word-painting** — on *drop*, nine descending notes on weak off-beats in **bars 23 to 25**, illustrating the snakes falling from Alecto's head — alongside **melismatic** writing set against syllabic. The song's singer likewise never sings a repetition the same way twice, beginning **syllabic** and within a sixth and becoming steadily more melismatic, with flattened thirds and sevenths.

Purcell, though, has a second changing layer: the continuo realisation above the ground is elaborate and varies too. So he has two moving parts over one fixed one where the song has a single moving part over two fixed ones. That gives Purcell more room, and it is why his extract can afford a chromatic bass without becoming crowded.

**Context.** The ground bass was a Baroque commonplace, and Purcell was regarded as a master of it; Pachelbel's and Handel's grounds work on the same principle, and the ground's popularity is part of why the aria is short, self-contained and able to stand alone as incidental music for a play. The repeating chord loop is equally standard in modern popular song, where its purpose is to get out of the singer's way. Neither composer is being ingenious in choosing the device; the interest is entirely in what they do with it.

**Conclusion.** Both sustain interest effectively, but by opposite routes, and each is better at a different thing. Purcell's chromatic ground keeps the harmony unsettled and shares the interest between voice and continuo, so his extract sustains **tension** more effectively. The song's deliberately plain loop concentrates everything on the singing, so it directs **attention** more effectively. Where Purcell varies what sits above a fixed bass, the song varies the singer against a bass that has already agreed not to compete.

questions.prompt: Appendix 5 defines the command words. What does "compare" require?
options: Similarities and differences, with relative judgements
Points that may or may not be linked together
Points joined to a justification or an extension
Recall of factual information, found or remembered
questions.solution: *Compare* is defined as "make points about the similarities and differences" and "make relative judgements". The second is *describe*, the third is *explain*, the fourth is *state, give, name, identify, list*. Relative judgements are the part students miss: it is not enough to list what is the same and what is different.

markScheme.description: similarities and differences, with relative judgements

questions.prompt: A Section B answer covers both extracts, evidences most of its points and compares them accurately, then summarises. What would most raise it from level 3 to level 4?
options: A conclusion that takes a position, with comparisons that build towards it
More musical elements covered, at a sentence or two each
Rarer technical terms in place of the ones already used
A longer opening setting out both pieces in their periods
questions.solution: Level 4 asks for "a cohesive critical argument" that demonstrates the ability to compare, contrast and draw conclusions, where level 3 asks only for "some attempt" at them. An answer that compares and then summarises is a list with an ending; one that decides its position first and selects comparisons for it is an argument. Adding more elements thins the answer, and unusual vocabulary is not what "sophisticated" means.

markScheme.description: a conclusion that takes a position, with comparisons serving it

questions.prompt:
**Extract A, familiar.** John Williams: *Star Wars* main title, from the Music for Stage and Screen area of study.

**Extract B, unfamiliar.** A film cue for a scene in which a character looks back at the home they are leaving.

**On the page:** four sharps in the key signature; three crotchets in a bar; a slow tempo, quiet throughout.

**What you hear:**

- A solo oboe carries the melody over sustained strings. It moves by step almost throughout and stays inside a sixth, in balanced four-bar phrases that rise and then fall.
- A harp plays the same rising arpeggio figure every two bars.
- At bar 17 a solo horn takes the same melody an octave lower, with the strings now in four parts underneath it.
- At bar 25 the music moves to the relative minor for eight bars, then returns.
- The cue ends on a chord of A moving to a chord of E, held very quietly.

Evaluate how effectively each piece uses melody and instrumentation to establish the mood its scene requires.
questions.solution:
**Melody.** The two themes are built from opposite materials. Williams's main title opens by leaping up a **perfect fifth**, from tonic B flat to dominant F, and the bars that follow drive up through **triplet quavers** into a leap of a **minor seventh**, with a tied minim holding the tension across the beat. Wide, open, rising intervals sound bold in a way a small step cannot, and the theme is made to be remembered and sung. The cue's oboe melody does the reverse: it moves **by step almost throughout**, stays inside a **sixth**, and falls into balanced four-bar phrases that rise and then come back down. A narrow, conjunct line that always returns to where it started is the melodic equivalent of looking back, which is exactly the scene it accompanies.

Both themes, though, are treated the same way: each returns carried by a different instrument. Williams's is doubled across three octaves in strings, horns and trumpets when it comes back, so it sounds enormous; the cue's is taken at bar 17 by a **solo horn an octave lower**, so it sounds more distant. The technique is the **leitmotif** principle in both cases — a theme that can return changed and so comment on what has happened — but one transformation amplifies and the other withdraws.

**Instrumentation.** The main title gives the theme to **high trumpets** at a fortissimo dynamic, with syncopated offbeat chords in the brass, lower strings and bassoons, and the rhythm reinforced by snare drum. Brass has been the sound of ceremony and heroism for centuries, so the listener hears a hero before seeing one. The cue uses a **solo oboe** over sustained strings, with a **harp** arpeggio figure every two bars. A single reed instrument playing quietly is heard as one voice rather than a crowd, and the sustained strings give it nothing to push against, so the scene stays private.

What both share is the full **late-Romantic symphony orchestra** and a willingness to let one timbre carry the identity of a theme. What they do not share is weight: Williams doubles until the sound fills everything available, and the cue never lets more than four string parts accumulate under one melody line.

**Tonality, metre and harmony.** The main title is firmly in **B flat major**, so the tonality never sounds in doubt even though many of its chords are built in fourths rather than in thirds, and its steady **four-four** with dotted and triplet rhythms makes it march. The cue is in **E major**, entirely diatonic, in **three-four** at a slow tempo, and its one harmonic event is a move at bar 25 to the **relative minor**, C sharp minor, which shares the key signature and so needs no new accidentals — a shadow rather than a change of scene. It ends with a chord of A moving to a chord of E, that is **IV to I**, a **plagal cadence**: softer and less final than a perfect cadence, which suits a scene that is not resolved, only left.

The contrast in metre does as much work as the contrast in melody. Four-four with dotted rhythms is a march, and marching is what heroes do. Three-four at a slow tempo cannot march; it can only sway.

**Context.** Both belong to the same tradition. Williams deliberately revived the full symphonic, late-Romantic sound of Golden Age Hollywood composers such as **Korngold**, at a time when many films used pop scores, and took the leitmotif from Wagner; the quiet cue uses the same orchestra and the same technique for the opposite purpose. Howard Shore's *Lord of the Rings* cues show both sides of the same practice — the same orchestra announcing and withdrawing — which is why the two extracts here sound like relatives rather than strangers.

**Conclusion.** Each is highly effective, and each works by refusing what the other does. Williams needs the audience to recognise a hero instantly and never forget the tune, so he uses the loudest timbre, the widest intervals and the most certain tonality available, and repeats the theme until it is unmissable. The cue needs the audience to feel something private and unfinished, so it uses one quiet instrument, the narrowest melodic range, a metre that cannot march and a cadence that declines to close. Of the two, the cue is the more precisely judged, because restraint gives a composer fewer tools and less room for error; but the main title is the more effective at what it was written to do, since it has to survive being played over a scrolling caption with no picture to help it.

examTechnique.body:
**Know the question before you see it.** Section B is a single **12-mark** question: compare one **set work** with one **unfamiliar piece** related to a set work. Scores for both are printed in a source booklet. In the 2021 paper the pair was played **three times each, alternating** familiar and unfamiliar.

**Write about both pieces.** The mark scheme caps a one-piece answer at **6 out of 12**. This is the single most expensive mistake available in Section B, and it is entirely avoidable.

**Half the marks are for knowing, half for judging.** AO3 is 6 marks for musical knowledge, vocabulary and evidence. AO4 is 6 marks for evaluation, comparison and conclusions. An appraising point is credited only where a musical observation supports it.

**Plan by element.** Texture, melody, tonality and harmony, rhythm, sonority, structure, context. Pick three or four and take both pieces through each one.

**Use the scores.** They are printed for a reason. A bar number is evidence, and evidence is what separates level 3 from level 2.

**Name the period and the style.** Stylistic awareness is written into the level 3 and level 4 descriptors. Saying *Baroque* and meaning it — continuo, ground bass, terraced dynamics — is worth more than another adjective.

**Reach for wider listening once.** One sentence putting a piece beside another work of its kind earns credit and costs nothing.

**Finish with a conclusion.** The top level asks for a cohesive critical argument. Two or three sentences that answer the actual question — which piece does the thing better, and why — turn a list of comparisons into an argument.
examinerErrors: Writing about the set work only, or nearly only, which caps the answer at half marks however good it is.
Describing each piece in turn, so nothing is ever actually compared.
Making judgements with no musical feature attached: "it is exciting", "it is sad", "I preferred the second one".
Naming features with no judgement at all, which throws away the six AO4 marks.
Ignoring the printed scores, so no evidence of any kind reaches the page.
Retelling everything known about the set work, most of which the question did not ask about.
Using the vocabulary of one area of study for a piece from another.
Stopping when the last comparison is made, with no conclusion drawn.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer covers both pieces from the first paragraph and never lets one of them drift out of view. It is organised by musical element rather than by piece, so every paragraph compares rather than describes. Each point names a feature, supports it from the printed score, and then judges its effect — in that order, because the mark scheme credits appraisal only where an observation supports it. It uses the right vocabulary for each piece's own tradition, places both in their period and style, and finds room for one accurate reference to other music it has studied. It ends with a conclusion that answers the question asked, not a summary of what was already said.
